body:
A large empire with diverse people

Ashoka was the third major ruler of the Mauryan dynasty, which governed a large part of the Indian subcontinent during the 3rd century BCE. The empire was founded by Chandragupta Maurya around 321 BCE. He was succeeded by his son Bindusara, who was followed by Ashoka.

The imperial capital was Pataliputra, near present-day Patna in Bihar. Important provincial centres included Taxila, Ujjayini, Tosali and Suvarnagiri. The empire contained cities, agricultural villages, forest communities and populations following different religious traditions. People also spoke different languages and observed different customs.

Such diversity created a practical challenge for imperial government. The emperor could issue orders from the capital, but maintaining peaceful relations among communities and communicating with people over long distances required more than military power. Ashoka attempted to address these concerns through a policy he called dhamma.

What was dhamma?

Dhamma is the Prakrit form of the Sanskrit word dharma. In Ashoka's public inscriptions, it refers chiefly to a practical code of moral conduct: kindness, respect for elders, generosity, restraint from harming living beings and respect for different religious traditions.

Ashoka's dhamma was intended to guide everyday conduct and improve relations among people. It was not presented as a new religion requiring everyone to worship a particular deity or perform a prescribed sacrifice.

Ashoka was personally devoted to Buddhism, but his general public teaching of dhamma was broader than instructions intended specifically for Buddhist monks and nuns. This distinction is important: the emperor's personal religious allegiance and the ethical policy addressed to his diverse subjects were related but not identical.

The ruler's messages on stone

Ashoka communicated many of his instructions by having them engraved on natural rock surfaces and stone pillars. Such royal proclamations are called edicts. They discussed moral conduct, administration, religious relations and welfare measures.

In many inscriptions, the ruler identifies himself as Devanampiya Piyadasi. These titles are commonly translated as Beloved of the Gods and pleasant to behold, respectively. His personal name, Ashoka, occurs in some other inscriptions. Therefore, the absence of the name Ashoka from an inscription does not necessarily mean that another ruler issued it.

The inscriptions are particularly valuable because they preserve instructions issued in the ruler's own name. Nevertheless, an inscription stating what people should do is evidence of a royal instruction, not proof that every person obeyed it.

Prelims focus

  • The Mauryan succession was Chandragupta Maurya, Bindusara and Ashoka.
  • Pataliputra was the imperial capital.
  • Ashoka's dhamma emphasised ethical conduct and social harmony.
  • Devanampiya Piyadasi was a royal designation used in Ashokan inscriptions.
  • Ashoka's messages were engraved on both rocks and pillars.
  • Trap: Ashoka's general dhamma policy was not simply an order that every subject must become Buddhist.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 8, Ashoka, the Emperor Who Gave Up War, printed pp. 75–80; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Chapter 2, Kings, Farmers and Towns, printed pp. 32–34 and 47; S. Dhammika, The Edicts of King Asoka, Introduction and Minor Rock Edicts, consulted 18 November 2026.]

title: Ashoka, the Mauryan Empire and the Meaning of Dhamma

body:
The conquest of Kalinga

Kalinga was an ancient region on the eastern coast of India, principally associated with present-day coastal Odisha. Ashoka conquered it in the 8th year after his coronation, generally placed in the middle of the 3rd century BCE.

The conquest is important because Ashoka's own account records not merely a military victory but also his distress at its human consequences. The principal source for this event is Major Rock Edict 13.

The losses recorded in Major Rock Edict 13

Ashoka's inscription gives the following figures for the conquest:

  • 150,000 people deported, meaning removed from their homes or taken away after the conquest.
  • 100,000 people killed.
  • Many more people died from other causes associated with the war and its consequences.

These figures are the numbers reported in the royal inscription. They should be understood as Ashoka's recorded account, rather than as independently verified population statistics.

The inscription also describes suffering among people who were not directly killed or deported. Families lost relatives, religious communities were disrupted, and survivors experienced grief when friends and neighbours suffered. Ashoka declared that these consequences caused him deep remorse.

From military conquest to dhamma-vijaya

Dhamma-vijaya means conquest or victory through dhamma. In Ashoka's policy, it meant gaining goodwill and moral influence through righteous conduct and instruction rather than treating territorial conquest by force as the highest achievement.

Major Rock Edict 13 presents dhamma-vijaya as preferable to conquest through warfare. Ashoka wanted future rulers to avoid further military conquests and to value moral restraint.

This change also helps explain the expression found in Major Rock Edict 4: the sound associated with warfare is contrasted with the sound or proclamation of dhamma. The contrast expresses the change in the kind of achievement Ashoka wished to emphasise.

Did Ashoka completely abandon the use of force?

No. A distinction must be made between rejecting aggressive conquest as an ideal and abolishing all state power to punish or use force.

Major Rock Edict 13 itself indicates that Ashoka still recognised the state's power to punish, including in its dealings with forest communities. He urged restraint, forgiveness where possible and mild punishment. Thus, the inscription supports the conclusion that Ashoka changed his declared priorities; it does not support the claim that he dissolved his army or prohibited every use of force.

Why Kalinga matters to the history of dhamma

The Kalinga episode links warfare with Ashoka's wider moral programme. His concern about suffering provided a powerful reason to promote compassion, non-injury, fair treatment and peaceful relations. The same ideas later appeared in instructions to officials, public edicts and welfare measures.

Prelims focus

  • Kalinga was associated with present-day coastal Odisha.
  • Ashoka conquered Kalinga in the 8th year after his coronation.
  • Major Rock Edict 13 records the conquest and Ashoka's remorse.
  • The inscription reports 150,000 deported and 100,000 killed, with many more deaths.
  • Dhamma-vijaya means victory through dhamma rather than military conquest.
  • Trap: Ashoka's preference for dhamma-vijaya did not mean that all punishment or state coercion was abolished.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 8, printed p. 79; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Chapter 2, Source 11, printed p. 48; S. Dhammika, The Edicts of King Asoka, Major Rock Edicts 4 and 13, consulted 18 November 2026.]

title: The Kalinga War: Remorse and the Idea of Dhamma-vijaya

body:
A practical code of conduct

Ashoka's dhamma sought to improve the behaviour of individuals and the relationships among groups within the empire. It addressed problems such as family quarrels, harsh treatment of servants, religious hostility and injury to living beings.

Its central principle was that good conduct mattered more than an impressive outward display of religious observance. The teachings could be understood and practised by people belonging to different communities.

The principal duties taught by Ashoka

Respect within families and society

Ashoka emphasised respect for parents, elders and teachers. He also encouraged proper conduct towards relatives, friends and neighbours. These duties were meant to reduce conflict and strengthen cooperation in everyday life.

Kind treatment of servants and dependants

Slaves, servants and employees were to be treated with consideration rather than cruelty. This was a particularly important part of Ashoka's moral teaching because people in dependent positions could be vulnerable to mistreatment.

The principle required humane behaviour. It should not be confused with a declaration that Ashoka abolished the institutions of slavery or social hierarchy.

Generosity and concern for others

Ashoka encouraged gifts and assistance to relatives, friends, Brahmanas and shramanas. Brahmanas were associated with Brahmanical religious traditions, while shramanas included renouncers and ascetics who pursued religious or spiritual disciplines.

Generosity was not confined to members of the emperor's own religious community. It reflected his broader concern for ethical relations among different groups.

Compassion towards living beings

Ashoka advised restraint in harming or killing animals. He discouraged animal sacrifice and imposed restrictions on certain forms of slaughter.

However, the inscriptions do not establish a complete and immediate prohibition of all animal killing throughout the empire. Major Rock Edict 1 describes a reduction in animals killed for the royal kitchen, while Major Pillar Edict 5 provides specific protections for particular animals and occasions.

Truthfulness, self-control and purity of conduct

Dhamma also required individuals to examine their own behaviour. Truthfulness, gratitude, moderation, control of anger and avoidance of jealousy were valuable because they helped prevent harm to others.

Major Pillar Edict 2 identifies kindness, generosity, truthfulness and purity among the qualities of dhamma. Major Pillar Edict 3 urges people to recognise their own faults rather than notice only their good deeds.

Moral conduct and ritual practices

People observed rituals at important moments such as births, marriages, illnesses and journeys. Major Rock Edict 9 questions the usefulness of many such ceremonies and argues that the lasting benefit comes from ethical behaviour.

For example, an individual might perform a ceremony to seek good fortune while continuing to treat servants harshly. Ashoka's teaching places greater value on correcting the harsh treatment than on performing the ceremony alone.

This did not mean that every religious ceremony was forbidden. The important distinction was between ritual observance and the moral conduct that Ashoka considered more fruitful.

The gift of dhamma

Major Rock Edict 11 praises dhamma-dana, or the gift of dhamma. The idea is that encouraging proper conduct, respect and generosity benefits people in a lasting way. The edict contrasts this moral benefit with the more limited importance of ordinary gifts.

Dhamma was a code of conduct, not merely a form of worship. Its duties concerned family life, social relations, treatment of dependants, respect for religious communities and compassion towards living beings.

Prelims focus

  • Respect for parents and elders was a central duty of dhamma.
  • Kindness towards slaves and servants formed part of Ashoka's teaching.
  • Major Rock Edict 9 contrasts ethical conduct with ceremonies of limited benefit.
  • Major Rock Edict 11 emphasises dhamma-dana, the gift of dhamma.
  • Major Pillar Edict 2 describes kindness, generosity, truthfulness and purity.
  • Trap: Restraint on animal killing was not identical to a universal ban on every form of slaughter.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 8, printed pp. 80–81; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Chapter 2, printed p. 32; S. Dhammika, The Edicts of King Asoka, Major Rock Edicts 1, 3, 9 and 11, and Major Pillar Edicts 2, 3 and 5, consulted 18 November 2026.]

title: The Principles of Ashoka's Dhamma in Everyday Life

body:
Why religious harmony mattered

The Mauryan Empire contained people following different religious traditions. These included Brahmanical practices, Buddhism, Jainism and other ascetic movements. Disagreements between religious communities could become sources of hostility.

Ashoka's policy of dhamma attempted to reduce such conflicts by encouraging respectful conduct between followers of different traditions. He did not require people to have identical beliefs or abandon their own religious practices.

Major Rock Edict 7: coexistence of religious traditions

Major Rock Edict 7 expresses Ashoka's wish that different religious communities should be able to live throughout his dominions. It identifies self-control and purity of mind as values recognised across religious traditions.

The important point is that shared moral conduct could exist despite differences in religious belief. Ashoka did not present religious uniformity as the necessary condition for peaceful society.

Major Rock Edict 12: restraint in speech

Major Rock Edict 12 explains religious tolerance more directly. It warns that excessive praise of one's own religious tradition, accompanied by criticism of another without proper reason, can damage both.

Ashoka therefore encouraged people to:

  • Respect religious traditions other than their own.
  • Avoid insulting another community merely to glorify their own.
  • Exercise restraint when speaking about religious differences.
  • Listen to and learn about the teachings followed by others.

The edict does not forbid every form of disagreement. It indicates that, when criticism has a proper basis, it should be expressed mildly. Its central concern is the avoidance of needless hostility.

Religious tolerance is not the same as religious uniformity. Ashoka encouraged respect and peaceful coexistence while recognising that different communities could continue to follow different teachings.

Ashoka's Buddhism and his treatment of other groups

Ashoka's personal commitment to Buddhism is visible in inscriptions addressed specifically to Buddhists. The Bhabru or Bairat Minor Rock Edict, for example, expresses his faith in the Buddha, the dhamma and the Sangha, and recommends certain teachings for Buddhist followers.

This differs from the general rock edicts, which address ethical conduct across communities. His personal Buddhism therefore should not be mistaken for an order compelling all subjects to accept Buddhist teachings.

Ashoka also extended patronage beyond Buddhism. Inscriptions at the Barabar caves in Bihar record donations associated with the Ajivikas, another ascetic religious group. His public instructions also supported respectful treatment of Brahmanas and other renouncers.

These examples show the practical meaning of tolerance: a ruler could hold a personal religious belief while asking officials and subjects to respect other traditions.

The administrative side of tolerance

Religious harmony was not presented merely as private advice. Major Rock Edict 5 describes the work of dhamma-mahamattas, special officials concerned with the promotion of dhamma and the welfare of people belonging to different religious communities.

Major Rock Edict 12 also mentions officials involved in promoting respectful relations. Thus, Ashoka linked the ethical principle of tolerance with official responsibilities.

Prelims focus

  • Major Rock Edict 7 concerns the coexistence of religious traditions.
  • Major Rock Edict 12 stresses restraint in speech and respect for other religions.
  • The Bhabru or Bairat Minor Rock Edict expresses Ashoka's personal Buddhist devotion.
  • Barabar cave inscriptions are associated with donations to the Ajivikas.
  • Dhamma-mahamattas worked for dhamma and welfare across religious communities.
  • Trap: Ashoka's support for Buddhism did not make his general public dhamma instructions exclusively Buddhist.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 8, printed pp. 80–81; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 3, Arts of the Mauryan Period, printed p. 20; S. Dhammika, The Edicts of King Asoka, Major Rock Edicts 5, 7 and 12 and Minor Rock Edict 3, consulted 18 November 2026; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Serial Nomination for Ashokan Edict Sites along the Mauryan Routes, description of Barabar cave inscriptions, submission dated 11 February 2025, consulted 18 November 2026.]
